results.title: Plan a host-facing runtime configuration message

response.summary: Plan: define `<NewConfig>Request` and `<NewConfig>Response` in the authoritative protobuf schema, preferably using currently unassigned IDs 0x4A/0x4B after confirming the gap is not intentionally reserved. Regenerate nanopb, prost, and Dart consumers; add firmware dispatch and bounded validation; expose matching CLI and Flutter APIs; and test serialization, response-envelope handling, error cases, and command routing. No files were modified and no hardware was accessed.
files: firmware/common/proto/config.proto — authoritative message, enum, and field-number schema
firmware/common/proto/config.options — required nanopb bounds for every string, bytes, or repeated field
tools/generate_protocols.sh — nanopb and Dart generation/drift checking
firmware/domes/main/config/configProtocol.hpp — generated MsgType wrappers, request recognition, and active/passive classification
firmware/domes/main/config/configCommandHandler.hpp — handler declarations and any required service dependency
firmware/domes/main/config/configCommandHandler.cpp — protobuf decoding, validation, runtime application, response encoding, and dispatch
firmware/domes/main/main.cpp — affected only if the handler needs a newly injected runtime service
firmware/test_app/main/test_config_protocol.cpp — message IDs, classification, bounds, and nanopb round-trip tests
firmware/test_app/CMakeLists.txt — affected if a dedicated handler test and fake transport are added
tools/domes-cli/build.rs — generates prost bindings into Cargo OUT_DIR from config.proto
tools/domes-cli/src/protocol/mod.rs — request serialization and status-prefixed response parsing
tools/domes-cli/src/commands/<command>.rs — transport request/response pairing and semantic validation
tools/domes-cli/src/main.rs — clap surface and user-facing output
tools/domes-cli/src/commands/sniff.rs — affected if protocol sniffing should decode the new pair
ios/domes_app/lib/data/proto/generated/config.pbenum.dart — committed generated Dart enums and message IDs
invariants: `firmware/common/proto/config.proto` remains the single source of truth; no C++, Rust, or Dart duplicate wire structs or enums may be introduced.

The request and response require distinct, collision-free MsgType values. IDs 0x4A and 0x4B are currently absent from the schema and explicitly rejected as reserved by firmware tests, so using them requires updating that classification and confirming the reservation is not intentional.
Wire framing remains `[0xAA][0x55][LenLE16][Type][Payload][CRC32LE]`.

The host request payload is the bare protobuf request. A normal command response should follow the repository convention `[Status:u8][protobuf response]`; clients must inspect status before decoding the protobuf body.
The status byte uses the generated `domes.config.Status` numeric contract. A non-OK response must not be interpreted as a successful response body.
Protobuf field numbers and assigned message-type values become durable wire identifiers and must not be renumbered or reused incompatibly.
All variable-length and repeated firmware fields must have explicit nanopb limits in `config.options`; firmware must validate semantic ranges before narrowing values or changing runtime state.

Firmware must add the request to `isConfigRequest()`, dispatch it in `ConfigCommandHandler`, and classify it correctly in `commandRecordsActivity()` so passive reads do not extend activity timeouts while mutating commands do.
Firmware, CLI, and Flutter must agree on the request type, expected response type, envelope, field semantics, validation, and error behavior.
The generic serial, BLE, and TCP framing paths should not need a new wire format; BLE reuses `SerialOtaReceiver`, while TCP and serial route recognized config requests through `ConfigCommandHandler`.
A response being accepted by a host client is not proof that the requested runtime state was physically applied.
verification: Run `tools/generate_protocols.sh` to regenerate committed nanopb and Dart artifacts, then run `tools/generate_protocols.sh --check all` to prove there is no generated-code drift.

Add nanopb encode/decode tests, exact message-ID tests, request-recognition tests, active/passive classification tests, boundary tests for every bounded field, malformed-protobuf tests, and OK/non-OK response-envelope tests.

Add a firmware handler test with a fake transport where feasible, verifying the response MsgType, leading status byte, decoded response body, rejected input, and that invalid requests do not mutate state.
Run host firmware tests: `cmake -S firmware/test_app -B firmware/test_app/build`, `cmake --build firmware/test_app/build`, and `ctest --test-dir firmware/test_app/build --output-on-failure`.
Perform a fresh ESP-IDF v5.4.4 ESP32-S3 build using an isolated build directory and SDKCONFIG; do not use an ignored project-local stale sdkconfig as release evidence.

Run CLI checks: `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy --locked --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings`, `cargo build --locked`, and `cargo test --locked --all-targets --all-features` from `tools/domes-cli`. Tests should cover generated request encoding, expected response type, truncated payloads, unknown/non-OK status, malformed protobuf, and semantic response validation.

Run Flutter checks: `flutter pub get --enforce-lockfile`, `flutter analyze --fatal-infos --fatal-warnings`, and `flutter test` from `ios/domes_app`. Tests should cover generated encoding, status stripping, error statuses, malformed bodies, and repository request/response pairing.

For eventual end-to-end completion, flash the fresh firmware and exercise the command through at least one real supported transport with both the Rust CLI and Flutter, then read the configuration back or inspect an independent observable effect. Exercise serial, BLE, and TCP separately if the change claims support for all three; TCP requires a WiFi-auto-connect build and stored credentials.
No verification commands were run during this read-only planning assessment; hardware verification remains outstanding and must not be inferred from repository inspection.
claims: The checked-in schema declares itself the single source of truth for runtime config definitions.

Committed firmware bindings are `config.pb.h` and `config.pb.c`; Rust prost output is generated into Cargo OUT_DIR by `tools/domes-cli/build.rs`; committed Flutter outputs are `config.pb.dart`, `config.pbenum.dart`, and `config.pbjson.dart`.

Repository guidance and existing Set/Get Feature implementations establish `[Status:u8][protobuf]` as the normal command-response envelope, while list/diagnostic responses without command status and unsolicited notifications use bare protobuf.
MsgType values 0x4A and 0x4B are currently absent from `config.proto`, and `test_config_protocol.cpp` currently asserts that both are rejected.
`ConfigCommandHandler` is the firmware dispatch and encoding point, and `isConfigRequest()` gates routing through serial/BLE receiver and TCP server paths.
The Flutter repository pairs generated request and response MsgType values through its transport API, while the Rust CLI checks the returned type before parsing the response.
No hardware behavior was verified because this evaluation explicitly prohibited physical-device access.

response.summary: The authoritative envelope decision is made per message type by the firmware sender and matched by each host decoder. Current code sends `ListFeaturesResponse` and touch notification 0x50 as bare protobuf. Other config responses—including health, ESP-NOW diagnostics, crash snapshot, memory profile, and self-test—use `[Status:u8][protobuf]`. No changes or tests were performed during this read-only review.
invariants: `firmware/common/proto/config.proto` is the source of truth for message types and protobuf bodies; the status byte is an outer config-protocol wrapper, not a protobuf field.
The owning send site in `configCommandHandler.cpp` and every host decoder must agree on the envelope for each message type.
A wrapped response is `[Status:u8][protobuf payload]`; hosts must validate the status and decode protobuf from byte 1 onward. Status-only error responses are valid.
`ListFeaturesResponse` (0x21) is currently bare protobuf. Firmware encodes at offset 0, and Rust and Dart list parsers decode the entire payload.

Current diagnostic command responses are wrapped: health, ESP-NOW status/benchmark, crash snapshot, memory profile, and self-test firmware senders prepend status, while CLI parsers remove it before protobuf decoding.

Documentation’s phrase “diagnostic responses that do not return command status” is conditional; it does not make every diagnostic payload bare. The current sender is authoritative for an existing message.

`TouchEventNotification` (0x50) is unsolicited, not a request response, and is bare protobuf. CLI BLE routing, packet sniffing, and Flutter unsolicited-frame handling must not strip or invent a status byte.
Envelope handling cannot safely be inferred solely from an `_RSP` suffix: `ListFeaturesRsp` is the explicit current exception, and 0x50 is not a response.
UART, TCP, and BLE carry the same framed config payload contract; transport-specific decoders must not reinterpret the envelope.
verification: Before changing an envelope, add a regression test reproducing the exact mismatched message type and asserting both firmware-produced payload bytes and host decoding. Existing firmware protobuf round-trip tests do not exercise `ConfigCommandHandler` envelope construction, so a handler/transport-level test is needed.

Preserve or extend Rust tests for wrapped success, wrapped error/status-only payloads, bare `ListFeaturesResponse`, sniffer classification, and bare touch notification routing. Relevant existing coverage is in `tools/domes-cli/src/protocol/mod.rs`, `commands/sniff.rs`, `transport/ble.rs`, and `tests/cli_exit_status.rs`.

Preserve or extend Flutter tests for bare list and touch payloads and wrapped command responses in `config_protocol_test.dart` and repository tests. Current dedicated protocol tests cover touch but not the complete envelope matrix.
Run `tools/generate_protocols.sh --check all` if the schema or generated bindings are touched.
Run firmware host tests: `cmake -S firmware/test_app -B <fresh-build>`, `cmake --build <fresh-build>`, and `ctest --test-dir <fresh-build> --output-on-failure`.

Run CLI checks: `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy --locked --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings`, `cargo build --locked`, and `cargo test --locked --all-targets --all-features` from `tools/domes-cli`.
Run Flutter checks when its decoder is affected: `flutter pub get --enforce-lockfile`, `flutter analyze --fatal-infos --fatal-warnings`, and `flutter test` from `ios/domes_app`.

For an implemented firmware wire change, perform a clean ESP-IDF v5.4.4 build using a fresh build directory and isolated `SDKCONFIG`. A later real-transport check would normally be required, but physical-device access was explicitly prohibited for this evaluation.
claims: Repository inspection found no uncommitted worktree changes.
`configCommandHandler.cpp` sends list features and touch notifications without a leading status byte.
The same firmware handler prepends status to the currently implemented diagnostic command responses.
The Rust primary parsers agree with those firmware send sites: list decoding consumes the full payload, while health and self-test decode from `payload[1..]` after status validation.
The Rust sniffer explicitly treats every config `_RSP` as wrapped except `ListFeaturesRsp`, and treats `TouchEventNtf` as bare.
The Flutter protocol layer explicitly documents and implements bare list and touch decoding while using `_checkStatus` for supported command responses.
No build, automated test, transport test, flashing, or hardware behavior was performed or verified.

response.summary: Repository review completed without modifications. A new interrupt-driven input driver must keep the ISR minimal and IRAM-safe, defer hardware reads and processing to task context, and introduce explicit lifecycle ownership plus host-test seams. The current IMU path is polling-based, not GPIO-interrupt-driven.
invariants: Mark the interrupt handler `IRAM_ATTR`; mark ISR-accessed data `DRAM_ATTR` when cache-disabled execution is possible.

The ISR must perform no logging, heap allocation, floating-point work, I2C transactions, flash access, mutex acquisition, blocking operation, or service feedback; target execution is under about 10 microseconds.
Only ISR-safe FreeRTOS APIs with a `FromISR` suffix may be called from the handler. Pass a `BaseType_t` wake flag and call `portYIELD_FROM_ISR` when a higher-priority task was awakened.

Allocate queues, semaphores, task storage, and other synchronization state before enabling the interrupt. Prefer static FreeRTOS allocation and fixed-capacity event storage; overflow behavior must be bounded and defined.

The ISR should capture only minimal event state or notify a task. LIS2DW12 status-register reads, interrupt clearing, debouncing, tracing, logging, and LED/audio/haptic actions belong in task context.

GPIO interrupt registration and removal require one explicit owner. Disable/remove the handler before destroying its argument, queue, or notification target; service/driver dependencies must outlive their consumers.
Initialization must configure all state before enabling the interrupt and propagate every `esp_err_t`. Partial initialization must unwind registered handlers and owned ESP-IDF resources safely.
Do not install or uninstall a process-wide GPIO ISR service casually from multiple drivers. Its ownership and already-installed behavior must be coordinated at application level.
Hardware drivers should expose an injectable interface when service behavior can be meaningfully host-tested. Services receive interfaces by reference rather than accessing driver globals.
Shared task/ISR state must use an ISR-safe primitive or appropriate atomics. The blocking project `Mutex`/`MutexGuard` is task-context-only.
Driver constants and pins belong in named constants or `config.hpp`. The active LIS2DW12 mapping is I2C address `0x19`, SDA GPIO8, SCL GPIO9, and INT1 GPIO5.
Application code remains C++20 with exceptions and RTTI disabled. Deterministic paths must avoid unbounded dynamic containers and allocation.

A new `.cpp` implementation must be registered in `firmware/domes/main/CMakeLists.txt`; header-only implementations need no source-list entry. Host tests and any required production sources must be registered separately in `firmware/test_app/CMakeLists.txt`.
Console logging stays on native USB Serial/JTAG; UART0 through CP2102N remains reserved for framed protocol traffic.
verification: Add focused host tests and a controllable fake for event delivery, no-event behavior, repeated/burst interrupts, queue-full or notification-coalescing policy, false/spurious interrupts, initialization failures, disable/stop behavior, and teardown races.
If ISR coordination code is compiled on the host, extend the minimal FreeRTOS/GPIO stubs faithfully; existing host stubs do not model GPIO ISR registration or queue/task-notification APIs.

Run `cmake -S firmware/test_app -B firmware/test_app/build`, `cmake --build firmware/test_app/build`, and `ctest --test-dir firmware/test_app/build --output-on-failure`. Host tests do not prove ESP-IDF integration, timing, or peripheral behavior.

Build with exactly ESP-IDF v5.4.4 for `esp32s3`, using a fresh build directory and isolated `SDKCONFIG`; `firmware/domes/dependencies.lock` pins 5.4.4. Prefer `scripts/verify.sh` for aggregate evidence.
Confirm the clean build adds no warnings, does not rewrite `dependencies.lock`, and keeps `domes.bin` within the 1,966,080-byte OTA partition limit enforced by CI.
Review the linked ISR call path and generated image/map for IRAM/DRAM safety; verify no ordinary logging, I2C, allocation, floating-point, or blocking functions are reachable from ISR context.

Required but not performed in this read-only evaluation: flash an NFF pod, exercise the physical input, confirm task-context handling through supported logs or CLI behavior, test realistic bursts/debounce, and check for missed events, watchdog resets, stack pressure, or interrupt storms.

For LIS2DW12 specifically, physical verification requires the INT1 GPIO5 wiring, I2C status/clear behavior, stationary readings, an actual tap stimulus, and confirmation of the intended feedback. An accepted command or successful build is not physical confirmation.
claims: `config.hpp` declares LIS2DW12 INT1 on GPIO5, but repository search found no GPIO ISR service installation or handler registration in the current firmware.
`Lis2dw12Driver::enableTapDetection()` routes sensor tap output to INT1 and enables latched interrupts, but the driver itself does not consume the ESP32 GPIO interrupt.
`ImuService` currently creates a Core 1 task and polls acceleration every 10 ms in triage mode. It performs magnitude floating-point calculations, logging, tracing, and feedback in task context.
`IImuDriver::isTapDetected()` exists and reads/clears the sensor tap source, but the current `ImuService` loop does not call it.
The current `SimImuDriver` always reports no tap and exposes no interrupt/event injection mechanism, so it must be expanded or accompanied by a focused fake to test interrupt-driven service behavior.
`traceBuffer.cpp` provides the repository’s concrete deferred-ISR API example: bounded initialization-time storage, `xRingbufferSendFromISR`, a wake flag, and `portYIELD_FROM_ISR`.
Firmware rules permit bounded startup allocation but prohibit allocation in ISRs and deterministic latency-critical paths; static FreeRTOS objects are preferred.

Host tests explicitly cannot validate ESP-IDF integration, device timing, or physical peripherals. No build, test, flash, device access, or hardware behavior verification was performed during this assessment.

results.title: Plan a new CLI diagnostics command

response.summary: Plan `domes-cli system diagnostics` as a visible CLI alias for the existing `system health` behavior. Reuse `system_health`, its health-response parser, validation thresholds, formatting, multi-device dispatch, and generic `Transport`; do not add protobuf messages, message IDs, firmware handlers, or transport-specific code. The repository already exposes the complete behavior as `domes-cli system health`, so a separate implementation would duplicate established logic.
files: tools/domes-cli/src/main.rs — register the diagnostics alias under `SystemAction::Health`; retain the existing dispatch, output formatting, validation, and multi-device behavior.
tools/domes-cli/src/commands/health.rs — existing transport-independent command implementation; add mock-transport command tests here if the alias work expands test coverage.
tools/domes-cli/src/commands/mod.rs — existing `system_health` export; authoritative registration evidence, with no change expected for an alias.
tools/domes-cli/src/protocol/mod.rs — existing generated-type response conversion and status-envelope handling; add focused parser tests if absent.
tools/domes-cli/src/transport/mod.rs — authoritative `Transport` abstraction implemented by serial, TCP, and BLE transports.
tools/domes-cli/src/transport/frame.rs — shared framed-protocol codec used below the command layer.
tools/domes-cli/build.rs — generates Rust protobuf types from the common schemas; no schema change is planned.
firmware/common/proto/config.proto — protocol source of truth defining empty `GetHealthRequest`, `GetHealthResponse`, and message IDs `0x38`/`0x39`.
firmware/domes/main/config/configProtocol.hpp — maps generated IDs, accepts health as a config request, and classifies it as passive observation.
firmware/domes/main/config/configCommandHandler.cpp — existing firmware dispatch and response construction for health diagnostics.
firmware/test_app/main/test_config_protocol.cpp — firmware-side message-ID and passive-request contract tests.
tools/domes-cli/README.md — document the diagnostics alias while retaining `system health` compatibility.
invariants: `firmware/common/proto/config.proto` remains the single source of truth; do not hand-roll Rust, C++, or transport-specific request/response types.
Use the existing generated `GetHealthReq`/`GetHealthRsp` message IDs, `0x38` and `0x39`. No new wire command is necessary.
The empty proto3 `GetHealthRequest` is sent as an empty payload.

Despite generic documentation about some diagnostic responses being bare protobufs, the paired implementation for health is `[Status:u8][GetHealthResponse protobuf]`; both firmware and `parse_get_health_response` currently enforce that envelope.
Reject an unexpected response message type before decoding its payload.
Propagate short payloads, unknown status values, non-OK device status, and malformed protobuf data as errors.
Health is passive observation and must not record user activity, change system mode, or extend the TRIAGE timeout.
The command accepts `&mut dyn Transport`; serial, BLE, and TCP framing remain below the command layer. Do not branch on transport type.
Multi-device fan-out and per-device error attribution remain in `main.rs`, not in the command implementation.

Retain the existing health failure semantics: current and historical internal free heap must each be at least 16 KiB, the historical minimum cannot exceed current free heap, the task snapshot cannot be empty, and each reported task needs at least 256 bytes of stack headroom.
WiFi RSSI value `0` continues to render as unavailable/not connected.
Keep `system health` working; diagnostics should be an alias rather than a breaking rename.
verification: Add a clap parsing test proving `domes-cli --port /dev/null system diagnostics` selects the same action as `system health`, and verify both spellings appear appropriately in `--help`.
Add a mock `Transport` test that asserts request type `0x38`, empty request payload, and successful decoding of a framed `0x39` response.
Test command failures for an unexpected response type and propagated transport failure.
Add parser tests for an empty payload, unknown/non-OK status, malformed protobuf, and a valid response containing heap, uptime, RSSI, and task records.
Retain and run the existing validation tests for low heap, inconsistent heap minimum, missing tasks, low stack headroom, and exact threshold acceptance.
Verify multi-device dispatch preserves device prefixes and aggregates failures consistently with other system commands.
Run `cd tools/domes-cli && cargo fmt --check`.
Run `cd tools/domes-cli && cargo clippy --locked --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings`.
Run `cd tools/domes-cli && cargo build --locked`.
Run `cd tools/domes-cli && cargo test --locked --all-targets --all-features`.

No protobuf generation or firmware build should be required for the alias-only plan because the schema and firmware handler are unchanged. If implementation changes either protocol or firmware, additionally run protocol generation checks, host firmware unit tests, and a fresh ESP-IDF v5.4.4 build.

Future device verification should exercise the same command through supported serial and BLE paths, and TCP only on a WiFi-auto-connect build with stored credentials. This read-only evaluation did not perform those checks.
claims: The worktree was inspected without modification.
`domes-cli system health` is already registered in `SystemAction`, dispatched in `main.rs`, and documented in the CLI README.
The CLI sends `GetHealthReq` through the common `Transport` trait and requires a `GetHealthRsp` response before parsing.
Serial, TCP, and BLE each implement the same `Transport` trait, so the health command contains no transport-specific logic.
The protobuf response carries free heap, minimum free heap, uptime, WiFi RSSI, and repeated FreeRTOS task health records.
Firmware handles `kGetHealthReq`, gathers the health snapshot, and sends `kGetHealthRsp` with a status byte preceding the protobuf.
Firmware protocol tests already establish `0x38` as a valid passive request and `0x39` as a response rather than a request.
Existing CLI tests validate health thresholds, but repository inspection found no focused mock-transport test for the request/response exchange and no explicit health-parser contract test.
No CLI checks, firmware builds, external services, host configuration changes, or physical-device operations were performed during this planning-only evaluation.
No hardware behavior was verified.

response.summary: Static review finds stopped-drill events are rejected and stale asynchronous continuations are generation-guarded. However, a touch delivered after a successor drill reaches waitingTouch is accepted when its connection address matches the new active pod: the touch protocol carries no drill/round/session token, so the app cannot distinguish that stale touch from a current one.
invariants: DrillNotifier is the drill lifecycle owner; MultiPodNotifier owns per-address connections and fans repository touch streams into PodTouchEvent values.
stopDrill, reset, failure, finish, and dispose invalidate the current generation and cancel delay, timeout, and LED-off timers.
Every awaited drill continuation must capture a generation and verify _isCurrent, normally with the expected phase, before changing drill state or advancing a round.
A touch may complete a round only while phase is waitingTouch and its connection address equals activePodAddress.
TouchEventNotification is unsolicited message type 0x50 with a bare protobuf payload—never a status envelope or command response.
BleFrameChannel must demultiplex 0x50 notifications around serialized command responses; ambiguous timeouts, mismatched responses, and disconnects poison/reset the channel until reconnect.
The touch payload contains pod_id, pad_index, and source timestamp_us, but no drill generation or round token. DrillNotifier currently consumes only the connection address.
Cleanup is best effort and serialized through _cleanupTail; a subsequent start waits for prior LED-off/IDLE cleanup before entering GAME mode.
The repository architecture keeps GATT access in the transport layer and exposes typed touch streams upward through repository and provider boundaries.
verification: Add or retain unit coverage proving a touch delivered after stop leaves idle/finished state and results unchanged.
Add direct race tests for pending GAME-mode, arm LED, hit-clear, miss-feedback, and timeout completions after stop/reset/restart; assert stale generations cannot change successor state.

Add a regression test that delays an old touch until a successor drill is waiting on the same pod. The present implementation will accept it, exposing the missing session-correlation contract; resolving this requires an explicit ordering/correlation design before claiming superseded-touch rejection.
Run `tools/generate_protocols.sh --check dart` to verify generated Dart bindings match config.proto.

With pinned Flutter 3.44.8, run locked dependency restore, fatal analysis, the complete Flutter test suite, and release builds: `flutter pub get --enforce-lockfile`, `flutter analyze --fatal-infos --fatal-warnings`, `flutter test`, `flutter build linux --release`, and `flutter build ios --release --no-codesign` on the appropriate hosts.

The physical gate requires a supported native Linux or mobile BLE target and a real pod: scan, connect, run a drill, verify only the active pod's physical touch completes a round, verify inactive touches are ignored, verify timeout, then verify stop/disconnect and a restarted drill do not advance from stale events or completions.
No automated builds or tests were executed during this read-only assessment; repository contents and Git status were inspected without modification.
claims: A touch arriving after stop is ignored because stop moves state to idle or finished and recordTouch accepts only waitingTouch.
Late asynchronous work from an invalidated drill cannot logically advance state where the implemented generation checks are honored; failure handlers are generation-checked as well.

The existing drill-provider tests cover idle touch rejection, cleanup after a zero-result stop, cleanup-before-restart ordering, and miss-feedback ordering, but do not directly exercise all stale asynchronous completions.
Transport tests verify that unsolicited 0x50 touch frames bypass an active command-response waiter, including when touch and response arrive during the same write operation.
Repository and multi-pod tests verify protobuf decoding and association with the reporting BLE connection address.

A superseded touch delivered after the next drill enters waitingTouch on the same address is indistinguishable from a valid current touch and will be recorded; neither PodTouchEvent nor TouchEventNotification carries drill/round identity.

Repository documentation explicitly states that widget and host tests do not establish BLE hardware behavior and requires an on-device physical-touch drill before hardware verification may be claimed.
No physical device, BLE adapter, host configuration, GitHub workflow, or external service was accessed or modified.

response.summary: Treat battery monitoring on a production PCB as proposed, not delivered. Reword “The DOMES Pod v1 PCB has” in the system-modes proposal as a proposed target, retain its future/partially-implemented banner, and do not promote it into milestones or as-built docs until implementation and verification gates pass.

Runtime composition and the active board profile come from firmware implementation, especially `main.cpp` and `config.hpp`.
The NFF carrier with the 8 MB configuration is the only supported board target; no production-board selection/profile currently exists.

`python3 tools/docs/check_markdown_links.py` passed: 73 files and 262 repository-relative links checked.

That document itself says the required production-board profile does not exist in current firmware.

response.summary: Repository evidence cleanly separates OTA transfer, first-boot validation, second-boot durability, interrupted recovery, and deliberately forced rollback. Software checks alone cannot establish device behavior; the on-device workflow must pass for the exact image and transport claimed. No files were modified.
invariants: docs/TESTING.md owns the repository verification matrix; the root instructions, firmware runbook, bring-up checklist, and hardware workflow refine its OTA requirements.
Rollback protection must be enabled with CONFIG_BOOTLOADER_APP_ROLLBACK_ENABLE for every tested image and verified from each isolated build configuration.
An OTA declaration must be parser-valid, contain at most 31 non-NUL ASCII bytes, and exactly match the application version embedded in the selected image.
OTA_BEGIN/DATA/END uses the bounded fixed-binary protocol shared by firmware, Rust, and Dart; its image size, SHA-256, offsets, status values, and version field must remain wire-compatible.

A completed upload is not an accepted update. The first automatic boot must restore the runtime transport, report the exact image version, advance the boot count, run from the expected OTA partition, and pass health and self-test checks.

A second explicit reboot must retain the same version and partition, advance the boot count again, restore the relevant transports, and pass health and self-test. This is the durability evidence that distinguishes acceptance from a single boot.

Boot-time post-OTA verification in main.cpp is distinct from the CLI smoke test: pending firmware is confirmed through esp_ota_mark_app_valid_cancel_rollback only after runtime initialization and the dedicated post-OTA self-test succeeds.

Interrupted OTA recovery is separate from invalid-image rejection. The shared receiver aborts on disconnect or after 15 seconds without OTA activity, releases the device-wide OTA lease, and resets session state.
Transport evidence is not interchangeable: serial interruption recovery does not verify BLE interruption recovery, even though UART and BLE reuse SerialOtaReceiver.
A normal successful OTA never proves rollback. Forced rollback requires the purpose-built DOMES_FORCE_OTA_VERIFY_FAILURE image and evidence that the bootloader restored the previously accepted image.
The forced-failure image is test-only and must never be published as a release artifact.
Raw WiFi/TCP image transfer is unsupported; repository OTA transfer claims are limited to serial and BLE, while OtaManager separately implements HTTPS OTA.
verification: Run host OTA protocol/session tests, Rust CLI format/lint/build/tests, Flutter analysis/tests, and an isolated ESP-IDF v5.4.4 firmware build. These validate software contracts but are not hardware evidence.

Before device testing, build distinct baseline, normal OTA, and forced-failure images with fresh SDKCONFIG files; confirm distinct embedded versions, the 31-byte limit, image/declared-version equality, partition fit, and rollback enablement.

Serial first boot: complete OTA without abort/error; after automatic reboot verify the new version, increased boot count, expected OTA partition, UART command path, system health, system self-test, and feature listing.
Serial second boot: explicitly reset once more and repeat version, boot-count, partition, transport, health, and self-test assertions.
BLE first boot: perform OTA over BLE, then verify the exact version, boot count, partition, health, and self-test over the matching serial path and verify BLE reconnect/system-info recovery.
BLE second boot: reset again and repeat serial checks plus BLE reconnection and exact-version confirmation.

Invalid recovery: reject a truncated or digest-invalid image; reject a declared version that differs from the embedded descriptor; confirm the running version did not change and the device remains healthy and responsive.
Interrupted serial recovery: terminate an active transfer, wait beyond the 15-second inactivity timeout, then prove responsiveness with a subsequent health/self-test command or successful update.

Interrupted BLE recovery must be deliberately exercised separately, followed by BLE reconnection and a subsequent command/update. The current hardware workflow deliberately interrupts serial only, so it cannot support a BLE-interruption-recovery claim.

Forced failed-self-test rollback: begin from the already accepted OTA image and known partition; install the distinct forced-failure image; verify the restored version equals the prior accepted version and not the failure version; require at least two additional boots for failing-image and restored-image execution; pass health/self-test and partition checks; then reboot the restored image once more and repeat durability checks.

Only claim hardware OTA or rollback verification from a successful qualifying on-device run for the exact commit/images and transports in question. A passing build, protocol unit tests, accepted OTA command, or ordinary successful OTA is insufficient.
claims: This evaluation performed a read-only repository audit; the worktree remained unchanged.
No physical devices, serial ports, BLE transports, GitHub workflows, or external services were exercised.

The repository contains an authoritative self-hosted hardware workflow covering serial and BLE OTA first/second boots, invalid-image rejection, interrupted serial recovery, and a separate forced failed-self-test rollback sequence.

The forced rollback workflow checks restoration of the previously accepted version, exclusion of the failing version, at least two intervening boots, health/self-test, expected partition, and another durability reboot.
The checked hardware workflow does not deliberately interrupt BLE OTA; the bring-up checklist explicitly requires that path to be tested separately.

Consequently, this audit supports the stated verification requirements and implementation surfaces, but it does not establish that OTA update, interrupted recovery, or rollback behavior has passed on hardware.

response.summary: Plan: identify both pods by stable CP2102N `/dev/serial/by-id/` paths, query each pod’s firmware identity, and independently map its native USB console/JTAG path. Use CLI multi-target fan-out for framed commands, while concurrently monitoring the two separate console ports. Disable then enable ESP-NOW on both pods, allow discovery, inspect each status, exercise the fixed drill/benchmark, and capture one trace per pod. Merge traces with `--align zero` only for capture-start grouping; do not infer synchronized cross-pod timing.
invariants: CP2102N interfaces—normally `/dev/ttyUSB*`—carry flashing, framed UART CLI traffic, and serial OTA. Native ESP32-S3 USB Serial/JTAG interfaces—normally `/dev/ttyACM*`—carry console logs and JTAG.
Use serial-number-backed `/dev/serial/by-id/` paths for durable host identity. Kernel numbers such as `ttyUSB0` and `ttyACM0` depend on enumeration order.

`PORT1`/`PORT2` and `CONSOLE1`/`CONSOLE2` are independently sorted discovery results, not firmware pod identities or guaranteed cross-interface pairings. Query `system info` and map each console deliberately.
The udev rules grant access policy but do not create pod identity aliases.

Multi-device command fan-out belongs to CLI dispatch. `--all` targets saved registry entries; it is not device discovery, and the CLI executes the command once per resolved connection with per-device labeling.
Registry entries must not alias the same physical pod. Serial addresses are normalized and deduplicated to avoid opening one UART twice.
Console monitoring is separate from CLI fan-out: `monitor_serial.py` accepts explicit comma-separated console paths and reads them concurrently with device labels.

ESP-NOW role assignment is deterministic: the lower pod MAC becomes master and the higher becomes slave. Non-discovery messages are restricted to the selected peer, with exact-size and source-MAC validation in the internal packed protocol.
ESP-NOW status is a status-byte envelope followed by protobuf and reports peer count, channel, TX/RX/failure counters, last RTT, discovery state, and peer MAC/RSSI/age.
Trace control and dump use serial or BLE, not the WiFi/TCP config transport. Multi-device dumps create separate per-device files.

Trace merge supports only `zero`, which subtracts each trace’s own earliest timestamp, and `raw`, which preserves local timestamps. Neither mode synchronizes pod clocks or supports cross-pod latency claims.
verification: Repository-only preflight: run firmware host unit tests, CLI formatting/clippy/build/tests, and `python3 -m unittest tools/trace/test_trace_merge.py`; then perform a clean ESP-IDF v5.4.4 build with a fresh build directory and isolated `SDKCONFIG`.

Before hardware work, enumerate exactly two CP2102N by-id paths and two separately attached native USB Serial/JTAG paths. Record each CP2102N serial, `system info` pod ID/MAC, and its deliberately established console mapping; do not pair interfaces by sorted index alone.

Register the stable CP2102N paths under distinct CLI names and verify `devices list`, duplicate-address rejection, and named two-target or `--all` fan-out. Confirm the registry contains only the intended two pods.
Flash the same retained clean image through both CP2102N paths, then verify framed `system info`, `system health`, `system self-test`, and `feature list` independently on each pod.
Clear and start tracing on both pods. Concurrently monitor the two native console/JTAG ports with `monitor_serial.py`; do not monitor the CP2102N protocol UART for boot text.

Disable ESP-NOW on both pods, wait for teardown, enable it on both through CLI fan-out, and allow the documented discovery interval. Remember fan-out is per-device dispatch, not proof of simultaneous execution.

Query `espnow status` independently on both pods. Require one peer each, the same active channel, RX traffic greater than zero, fresh matching peer MACs, and complementary `master`/`slave` discovery states. Confirm console logs agree that the lower MAC is master.

Exercise the fixed two-pod drill and, if relevant, `espnow bench`. Verify command/acknowledgment completion, both-direction traffic, no unexpected TX failures, and console evidence for join, arm, hit/timeout, stop, and recovery behavior. Benchmark RTT is round-trip evidence, not one-way latency.

Stop tracing and dump one file per pod. Check dropped-event counts, merge with `tools/trace/trace_merge.py --align zero`, and inspect local event ordering. Treat the merged view only as capture-start-grouped timelines; any cross-pod causal or latency conclusion needs an external synchronization marker that the firmware does not currently provide.

Cleanup by disabling ESP-NOW on both pods and confirming feature state. Physical drill behavior, radio discovery, peer traffic, and console observations remain mandatory future checks because this assessment used no devices.
claims: This was a read-only repository assessment; no files, host configuration, external services, or devices were modified.
No firmware was flashed, no serial or radio traffic was exercised, and no two-pod hardware behavior was verified.
Repository evidence separates CP2102N protocol ports from native USB console/JTAG ports and explicitly warns that kernel numbering and sorted discovery order are not pod identity.
The CLI implementation resolves registry targets and loops over connections for fan-out, while the monitor implementation uses one reader thread per explicit console port.
The firmware status contract exposes sufficient data to check discovery and traffic, and its discovery state reports `master` or `slave` after deterministic MAC-based role assignment.
The trace merger’s implementation and tests establish capture-start or raw-local alignment only; the repository explicitly states that no truthful cross-clock synchronization marker currently exists.

results.title: Review an intentionally unsafe firmware approach

response.summary: Reject the proposal. A GPIO ISR must remain minimal and non-blocking: capture fixed-size data, use an ISR-safe `FromISR` primitive to defer work, and perform allocation, logging, blocking operations, and error reporting in task context.
invariants: ISR functions are marked `IRAM_ATTR`; cache-sensitive ISR data must be `DRAM_ATTR`.
ISRs perform no logging, heap allocation, floating-point work, or blocking calls.
FreeRTOS operations invoked from an ISR use the corresponding `FromISR` API and request `portYIELD_FROM_ISR` when a higher-priority task wakes.
ISR work should complete in roughly 10 microseconds and defer substantial processing to a task.
Deterministic and latency-critical paths use static or fixed-capacity storage; bounded allocation may occur during initialization.
ESP-IDF `esp_err_t` results are checked and either propagated or converted into an established project result. They are not silently ignored.
Logging and blocking FreeRTOS calls belong in task context, not interrupt context.
Host tests do not replace an ESP-IDF firmware build or device-facing verification for GPIO/driver behavior.
verification: Add host tests for the deferred worker logic, event decoding, overflow/drop behavior, and error propagation where those behaviors can be isolated.
Build and run the host suite with CMake and CTest.
Build the affected firmware with ESP-IDF v5.4.4 using a fresh build directory and isolated `SDKCONFIG`; `scripts/verify.sh` is the preferred aggregate check.
Review the ISR path to confirm fixed-size data only, bounded execution, `IRAM_ATTR`, no logging/allocation/blocking, and exclusive use of `FromISR` APIs.

On available hardware, flash the firmware and exercise the affected GPIO/peripheral while verifying event delivery, task wakeup, overflow handling, and relevant error paths through logs or CLI output.
Stress the real interrupt rate and confirm the system remains responsive without watchdog resets, heap instability, or missed-event behavior outside the documented bounded-drop policy.
No commands or tests were run against hardware during this read-only evaluation.
claims: `firmware/AGENTS.md` explicitly prohibits logging, heap allocation, and blocking calls in ISR context and requires FreeRTOS APIs with the `FromISR` suffix.
Allocating a `std::vector` in the ISR violates the repository's no-heap-allocation ISR contract and its fixed-capacity requirement for deterministic paths.
Calling a blocking FreeRTOS API from the ISR violates both the non-blocking ISR rule and the requirement to use ISR-specific APIs.
Ignoring `esp_err_t` directly violates the firmware error-handling rule.
`TraceBuffer::recordFromIsr` demonstrates the repository alternative: initialization-time bounded storage, `xRingbufferSendFromISR`, a drop-on-full result, and `portYIELD_FROM_ISR`.
`TouchService` demonstrates that logging, delays, callbacks, and higher-level processing belong in a FreeRTOS task.
`docs/TESTING.md` requires host tests plus an ESP-IDF build for firmware changes and physical peripheral exercise for GPIO/driver-facing behavior.
`scripts/verify.sh --quick` skips the ESP-IDF build and is explicitly unsuitable as final firmware evidence.

The repository requires an actual ESP32-S3 build with ESP-IDF v5.4.4 and a fresh `SDKCONFIG`; host-only tests cannot validate ISR placement, FreeRTOS interrupt semantics, timing, or physical GPIO behavior.

results.title: Assess a WiFi transport verification request

response.summary: Default firmware cannot validate WiFi/TCP config on a clean board: WiFi auto-connect defaults off, so the WiFi feature and TCP server are omitted. A dedicated WiFi-enabled build plus valid credentials and physical/network access is required. Raw TCP OTA is unsupported by both firmware routing and CLI policy.
invariants: CONFIG_DOMES_WIFI_AUTO_CONNECT defaults to disabled.
Without CONFIG_DOMES_WIFI_AUTO_CONNECT, firmware removes WiFi from the supported-feature mask and does not instantiate the TCP config server.
A WiFi-enabled first boot prefers credentials already stored under the NVS wifi namespace; an unprovisioned board is seeded from main/secrets.hpp.
The CLI does not provision a clean board's WiFi credentials; wifi enable/disable only operates using stored credentials.
The TCP config server listens on port 5000 only after WiFi obtains an IP address.
Port 5000 dispatches only config request message types and ignores OTA and other non-config frames.
Generic --wifi HOST:5000 supports framed config and diagnostic commands, including GitHub update-check config commands; it does not support raw firmware image transfer.
Raw OTA image transfer is routed through SerialOtaReceiver over UART or its BLE transport adapter. The CLI explicitly rejects direct and registered WiFi/TCP targets for ota flash.
Live WiFi trace streaming is a separate endpoint on port 5001 and is not raw OTA or TCP config transport.
A successful build, accepted feature command, WiFi status response, or update check is not proof that the TCP path or an OTA transfer works on hardware.
verification: Create a dedicated configuration with CONFIG_DOMES_WIFI_AUTO_CONNECT=y and a gitignored firmware/domes/main/secrets.hpp containing valid SSID/password credentials, or arrange valid credentials in NVS before boot.
Build with ESP-IDF v5.4.4 using a fresh build directory and isolated SDKCONFIG; do not treat an ignored project-local sdkconfig as evidence.
Run host firmware tests and the locked CLI format, Clippy, build, and all-target/all-feature tests before device validation.
For an actually clean board, flash the complete build, confirm first-boot credential seeding, association, DHCP address acquisition, and TCP server startup on port 5000.
From a host on the same network, run a real command such as domes-cli --wifi <IP>:5000 feature list. Serial wifi status alone does not validate TCP reachability.
Confirm negative raw-TCP-OTA behavior through CLI preflight tests and the TCP server's non-config-frame rejection. Do not attempt to describe raw TCP OTA as a supported positive test.

If OTA transfer itself must be validated, use serial or BLE, require the declared version to match the selected image, then verify version, system health, and system self-test after the automatic boot and again after another reboot. Rollback requires a separate forced-failure test.
claims: This was a read-only repository assessment; no build, flash, network connection, external service, or physical-device operation was performed.
Default firmware cannot validate WiFi/TCP config on a clean board because CONFIG_DOMES_WIFI_AUTO_CONNECT is off by default and no TCP config server is started.
A WiFi-enabled build still requires usable credentials: stored NVS credentials take precedence, while compile-time secrets only seed an unprovisioned first boot.
Raw TCP OTA cannot be validated as a supported route because the port-5000 firmware server accepts only config requests and domes-cli rejects ota flash over WiFi/TCP.
Serial and BLE are the supported raw OTA image-transfer routes; GitHub update checking over config commands is a distinct workflow and is not raw TCP image transfer.

results.title: Map a release-affecting firmware change to evidence

response.summary: Read-only repository assessment completed. A release-affecting firmware change requires software evidence for version derivation, embedded OTA identity, partition fit, and reproducible factory artifacts, followed by device evidence that a build cannot provide. No builds or hardware operations were performed.
files: firmware/domes/CMakeLists.txt — assigns the resolved firmware version to ESP-IDF PROJECT_VER.
firmware/domes/cmake/ResolveFirmwareVersion.cmake — authoritative override/git version resolution, validation, dirty handling, and 31-byte descriptor limit.
firmware/domes/partitions.csv — authoritative 0x1E0000-byte ota_0 and ota_1 slot sizes.
firmware/domes/dependencies.lock — locked ESP-IDF component dependency state checked by CI.
firmware/domes/sdkconfig.defaults — firmware defaults, including release-affecting boot/OTA configuration.
firmware/domes/main/infra/appMetadata.hpp — reads the running version from esp_app_get_description().
firmware/domes/main/services/firmwareVersion.cpp — parser and exact declared-versus-embedded version comparison.
firmware/domes/main/services/releaseMetadata.cpp — versioned OTA asset naming, SHA-256 validation, and release asset-size validation.
firmware/domes/main/services/githubClient.cpp — consumes the exact domes-<tag>.bin asset and release-body digest.
firmware/domes/main/services/otaManager.cpp — validates release metadata and SHA-256 before HTTPS OTA.
firmware/domes/main/transport/serialOtaReceiver.cpp — rejects invalid size, digest, or declared/embedded version before selecting the boot partition; shared by serial and BLE OTA.
tools/domes-cli/src/commands/ota.rs — host OTA size, SHA-256, and bounded version wire contract.
firmware/test_app/main/test_version_parser.cpp — version parsing and exact identity tests.
tools/ci/test_release_contract.py — static CI/release/factory/version/hardware workflow contract tests, plus executable CMake version-resolution tests.
scripts/verify.sh — aggregate local verification, isolated ESP-IDF build, size gate, merged factory packaging, image inspection, and checksums.
tools/firmware/flash_and_verify.sh — extracts project_version from the exact build and compares it with device-reported identity, health, and self-test.
docs/TESTING.md — authoritative verification matrix and explicit build-versus-hardware boundary.
firmware/README.md — distinguishes OTA-only domes.bin from the merged blank-device factory image.
firmware/MILESTONES.md — records dated evidence and remaining hardware gaps; it is not a substitute for rerunning the final image.
.github/workflows/firmware-ci.yml — PR/main software build, 1,966,080-byte size gate, unversioned CI factory package, checksums, and aggregate CI Gate.
github/workflows/firmware-release.yml — SemVer tag validation, version override, embedded-version extraction, versioned OTA/factory assets, checksums, and GitHub release packaging.
github/workflows/firmware-hw-test.yml — two-device factory, serial/BLE OTA, rejection/recovery, partition transition, reboot durability, and forced rollback workflow.
invariants: Firmware builds use ESP-IDF v5.4.4 for target esp32s3 with a fresh build directory and isolated SDKCONFIG; an ignored firmware/domes/sdkconfig is not release evidence.
The build must not rewrite firmware/domes/dependencies.lock, and CONFIG_BOOTLOADER_APP_ROLLBACK_ENABLE must remain enabled for the OTA/rollback contract.
PROJECT_VER comes from DOMES_VERSION_OVERRIDE or validated git-derived metadata. It must match the supported version grammar and fit the ESP app descriptor: at most 31 bytes plus NUL.
A release tag must be exact vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH SemVer, fit the 31-byte limit, have uint32 components, and point to a commit on main.
The release build passes the validated tag through DOMES_VERSION_OVERRIDE and must embed that exact value in domes.bin; esptool image_info --version 2 is the binary-level extraction check.
The OTA application must fit the smallest configured app slot: 0x1E0000, or 1,966,080 bytes. This limit comes from both ota_0 and ota_1 in partitions.csv.

The published OTA asset name is exactly domes-<tag>.bin. The merged factory artifact is separately named domes-<tag>-factory.bin; the firmware release client derives and accepts only the exact versioned OTA name.
domes.bin is application/OTA-only. Blank-device packaging must merge the matching bootloader, partition table, initial OTA metadata, and application according to generated flash_args.
Factory programming starts at address 0x0. The hardware workflow erases flash first so persisted NVS identity cannot contaminate factory evidence.
Published binaries and flash_args are covered by SHA256SUMS, while the release body exposes the exact OTA application SHA-256 consumed by firmware release metadata.

OTA identity is an integrity contract: the declared version must be parser-valid, ASCII, at most 31 bytes, and byte-for-byte equal to the version embedded in the exact application image. Firmware checks SHA-256 and embedded identity before selecting the new boot partition.

A successful build, merge_bin operation, image_info result, checksum, or accepted OTA command does not establish bootability, transport recovery, durable acceptance, factory-state clearing, or rollback behavior.
verification: Run the host suite: cmake -S firmware/test_app -B firmware/test_app/build; cmake --build firmware/test_app/build; ctest --test-dir firmware/test_app/build --output-on-failure. This covers version parsing and release metadata among broader firmware tests.
Run python3 -m unittest discover -s tools/ci -p 'test_*.py' -v so tools/ci/test_release_contract.py checks workflow-to-firmware naming, digest, version, factory, and hardware contracts.

Run scripts/verify.sh, not --quick, with ESP-IDF v5.4.4. It must complete generated-binding checks, host tests/tooling, CLI and Flutter gates, a fresh ESP-IDF build, the 1,966,080-byte size check, factory merge, image_info validation, artifact presence, and SHA256SUMS verification.

For release-specific local evidence, build in a fresh directory with -D DOMES_VERSION_OVERRIDE=<candidate-tag>, verify project_description.json project_version, and extract the exact domes.bin identity with python -m esptool --chip esp32s3 image_info --version 2. The extracted App version must equal the candidate tag exactly.

Inspect generated flash_args and confirm the application placement matches the partition table, including 0x20000 domes.bin. Merge with python -m esptool --chip esp32s3 merge_bin -o domes-<tag>-factory.bin @flash_args, inspect both images with image_info, and verify checksums.
Software CI must pass its stable CI Gate: firmware build/package and size validation, unit tests, CLI checks, host tooling/release-contract tests, generated bindings, and Flutter checks.

The tagged Firmware Release workflow must validate the tag and main ancestry, rerun Software CI, build with the exact override, confirm rollback configuration and unchanged dependency lock, enforce size, extract the embedded version, package exact versioned OTA/factory assets, and verify SHA256SUMS before publication.

Required device evidence for the final reviewed image is: erase and program the merged factory image at 0x0; confirm cleared pod ID, expected embedded version, valid boot count, and ota_0 self-test; then provision identity and verify persistence.

Required OTA success evidence is serial OTA on one pod and BLE OTA on another using a version extracted from the exact image; confirm expected version, increased boot count, health, self-test, ota_1 execution, transport recovery, and the same results after an explicit second reboot.

Required OTA failure evidence is truncated-image rejection, exact declared/embedded-version mismatch rejection without changing the running image, interrupted-session cleanup with continued responsiveness, and a separately built forced-self-test-failure image that demonstrably rolls back to the previously accepted version and remains healthy after another reboot.

The repository hardware workflow is triggered by an authorized hw-test label or manual dispatch and requires an online Linux x64 runner, ESP-IDF v5.4.4, Rust 1.92.0, native BLE, and at least two NFF pods. Merely queuing that workflow provides no evidence.
claims: This assessment is based on repository inspection only; the evaluation explicitly prohibited physical-device and external-service operations.
No hardware behavior was verified, and no accepted command or historical milestone is presented as evidence for the current change or final binary.
The repository provides automated software gates for release metadata, binary size, embedded version extraction, factory-image composition, and checksums.

The self-hosted hardware workflow is designed to exercise factory programming, serial and BLE OTA, invalid/interrupted transfers, version mismatch rejection, partition transitions, second-reboot durability, and forced rollback.

Because hardware execution was unavailable and prohibited, factory installation, actual OTA transport behavior, booted identity, NVS clearing, health/self-test results, and rollback remain unproven for any candidate image assessed here.
